'''''Raphanus raphanistrum''''', also known as '''wild radish''', '''white charlock''' or '''jointed charlock''',<ref name = GRIN>{{GRIN}}</ref> is a [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Brassicaceae]]. The species is native to western Asia, Europe and parts of Northern Africa. It has been [[introduced species|introduced]] into most parts of the world and is regarded as a habitat threatening [[invasive species]] in many areas, for example, Australia. It spreads rapidly and is often found growing on roadsides or in other places where the ground has been disturbed. The cultivated [[radish]], widely used as a [[root vegetable]], is sometimes considered to be one of its subspecies as ''Raphanus raphanistrum'' subsp. ''sativus''.

==Description==
[[File:Raphanus raphanistrum petals.jpg|thumb|The petals have a characteristic pattern of veins]]

Wild radish is an [[annual plant|annual]] that grows up to {{convert|75|cm}} tall, variously branched to multi-stemmed, with a distinct slender [[taproot]] which does not swell like that of the cultivated radish. The stems are green and sometimes purple at the base and nodes, round in cross section and slightly ridged, and bristly-hairy all over. It has a basal rosette of [[pinnate]] leaves to {{convert|38|cm|abbr=on}} long, with a 3-cm stalk (petiole) and a large rounded terminal lobe that has a undulate margin; the lateral lobes sometimes overlap the midrib. The stem leaves become progressively less lobed as they ascend, and more acutely serrated. Both the upper and lower surface of each leaf is roughly hairy, as are the leaf margins, which have minutely bulbous-based hairs projecting horizontally. The leaves have green or purple tips ([[hydathode]]s) on each tooth.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref><ref name=rich>{{cite book| last = Rich| first = T.C.G.| year = 1991| title = Crucifers of Great Britain and Ireland | place = London| publisher = Botanical Society of the British Isles| isbn = 0901158208}}</ref><ref name=Poland>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref>

[[File:Raphanus raphanistrum leaves.jpg|thumb|The basal leaves are often pinnately divided.]]

[[File:(MHNT) Raphanus raphanistrum - Habitus.jpg|thumb|Habitat and distribution]]

The flowering period is between May and October in northern Europe, or between June and August in Minnesota.<ref name=minnesota/> The [[inflorescence]] is a lax [[raceme]], terminal or arising from the leaf axil, up to 34 cm long with up to 42 flowers. The flowers have four white (sometimes yellow or purple) petals, up to 24 mm long, sometimes with dark veins (especially on the underside). Each petal has a rounded "limb" above a narrow "claw", both about the same length. The four upright sepals are shorter than the petals, green or purple, and have sparse bulbous-based hairs. There are 6 stamens (2 short and 4 long) and one style with two stigmas.<ref name="Stace" />

The fruits are borne on bristly-hairy pedicels about 3 cm long and held vertically (whether the rhachis is erect or sprawling). Each fruit consists of a pod with two segments: the lower one is about 1-2 mm long and sterile (just occasionally with one seed), while the upper one is up to 8 cm long and has 1–10 fertile segments ([[mericarp]]s), each containing one oval seed up to 3 mm long. At the tip of the pod is a sterile beak up to 2.5 cm long. The fruits are [[terete]], smooth or slightly ridged, and glabrous to roughly hairy, with a peppery taste. At the tip of the beak is the persistent, sessile white [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]].<ref name="rich" /><ref name="Stace" /><ref name=Rose>{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |date=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne |location=London|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0}}</ref>

===Similar species===
The flowers are very similar to those of the [[searocket]], which is found in some of the same regions (in the US) and is easily distinguished from it by having thinner, non-[[wiktionary:succulent|succulent]] stems and leaves.<ref name=Readers>{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=40 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=9780276002175}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
It was formally described by the Swedish botanist [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his seminal publication ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' in 1753<!-- page 669 -->.<ref>{{cite web|title=Brassicaceae ''Raphanus raphanistrum'' L.|url=https://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=217826-2|publisher=ipni.org|access-date=8 November 2017}}</ref><ref name="plantlist">{{cite web|title=''Raphanus raphanistrum'' L. is an accepted name|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2422367|website=23 March 2012|publisher=plantlist.org|access-date=8 November 2017}}</ref><ref name="Grin">{{cite web|title=Taxon: ''Raphanus raphanistrum'' L.|url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=30856|publisher=ars-grin.gov|access-date=8 November 2017}}</ref>

The [[genome]] of wild radish is estimated to be ~515 Mb in size,<ref name=Moghe2014>{{cite journal|title=Consequences of Whole-Genome Triplication as Revealed by Comparative Genomic Analyses of the Wild Radish ''Raphanus raphanistrum'' and Three Other Brassicaceae Species|journal=The Plant Cell|volume=26|issue=5|pages=1925–1937|date=May 2014|doi=10.1105/tpc.114.124297|pmid=24876251|first=Gaurav|last=Moghe|pmc=4079359}}</ref> whereas that of the edible variety is suggested to be ~539{{en dash}}574 Mb.<ref>{{cite journal |title =Evolution of Genome Size in Brassicaceae |last1=Johnston |first1= J. Spencer |display-authors=etal |journal= Annals of Botany |volume=95 |issue=1 |year=2005 |pages=229–235 |doi=10.1093/aob/mci016|pmid=15596470 |pmc=1950721 }}</ref><ref name=Mitsui2015>{{cite journal |title=The radish genome and comprehensive gene expression profile of tuberous root formation and development |last1=Mitsui |first1=Yuki |display-authors=etal |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=5 |article-number=10835 |year=2015 |doi=10.1038/srep10835 |doi-access=free|pmid=26056784 |pmc=4650646 |bibcode=2015NatSR...510835M }}</ref><ref name=Jeong2016>{{cite journal |title=Elucidating the triplicated ancestral genome structure of radish based on chromosome-level comparison with the Brassica genomes |last1=Jeong |first1=Young-Min |display-authors=etal |journal=Theoretical and Applied Genetics |volume=129 |pages=1357–1372 |year=2016 |issue=7 |doi=10.1007/s00122-016-2708-0|pmid=27038817 |s2cid=5764946 }}</ref> Several ''Raphanus raphanistrum'' genomes have been sequenced,<ref name=Moghe2014 /><ref name=Mitsui2015 /><ref name=Jeong2016 /> with one study reporting 98% coverage of the gene space.<ref name=Jeong2016 /> Researchers found evidence that the past whole-genome triplication that occurred before the divergence of ''Raphanus'' and ''Brassica'' has been followed by widespread gene loss in radish, resulting in the loss of ~38,000 genes from the wild radish genome.<ref name=Moghe2014 />

''Raphanus raphanistrum'' has several known subspecies including:
* ''Raphanus raphanistrum'' subsp. ''landra'' <small>(Moretti ex DC.) Bonnier & Layens</small><ref>{{cite web |title=Tropicos.org Missouri Botanical Garden |url=https://tropicos.org/name/100353047 |access-date=4 July 2021}}</ref> ('sea radish')
* ''Raphanus raphanistrum'' subsp. ''rostratus'' <small>(DC.) Thell.</small><ref>{{cite web |title=Tropicos.org Missouri Botanical Garden |url=https://tropicos.org/name/4104290 |access-date=4 July 2021}}</ref>
* [[radish|''Raphanus raphanistrum'' subsp. ''sativus'']] <small>(L.) Domin</small><ref name="plantlist"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Tropicos.org Missouri Botanical Garden |url=https://tropicos.org/name/100349679 |access-date=4 July 2021}}</ref>

The scientific name ''Raphanus'' derives from the [[Ancient Greek]] name for a radish, ραφανίς (raphanis).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Morwood |first1=J. |last2=Taylor |first2=J. |title=Pocket Oxford Classical Greek Dictionary |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |isbn=0-19-860512-9}}</ref> It has several common names including jointed charlock,<ref name=minnesota>{{cite web|title=''Raphanus raphanistrum'' (Jointed Charlock)|url=https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/flower/jointed-charlock|publisher=Minnesota Wildflowers |access-date=8 November 2017}}</ref> jointed radish, jointed wild radish, white charlock,<ref name=Readers/> and wild radish.<ref name="Grin"/><ref>{{PLANTS|id=RARA2|taxon=Raphanus raphanistrum|accessdate=18 October 2015}}</ref>

It is often erroneously identified as [[White Mustard|mustard]].

==Distribution and habitat==
It is [[native plant|native]] to temperate regions of North Africa, Europe and parts of Western Asia.<ref name="Grin"/>

===Range===
It is found in North Africa, within [[Macaronesia]], [[Madeira Islands]], [[Canary Islands]], [[Algeria]], [[Egypt]], [[Libya]], [[Morocco]] and [[Tunisia]]. Within Western Asia it is found in the [[Caucasus]], [[Armenia]], [[Azerbaijan]], [[Cyprus]], [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]], [[Iran]], [[Iraq]], [[Israel]], [[Jordan]], [[Lebanon]], [[Syria]] and [[Turkey]]. In eastern Europe, it is found within [[Belarus]], [[Moldova]] and [[Ukraine]]. In middle Europe, it is in [[Austria]], [[Belgium]], [[Czech Republic]], [[Germany]], [[Hungary]], [[Netherlands]], [[Poland]], [[Slovakia]] and [[Switzerland]]. In northern Europe, in [[Denmark]], [[Estonia]], [[Finland]], [[Ireland]], [[Isle of Man]], [[Latvia]], [[Lithuania]], [[Norway]], [[Sweden]] and [[United Kingdom]]. In southeastern Europe, within [[Albania]], [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]], [[Bulgaria]], [[Croatia]], [[Greece]], [[Italy]], [[Montenegro]], [[North Macedonia]], [[Romania]], [[Serbia]] and [[Slovenia]]. Also in southwestern Europe, it is found in [[France]], [[Portugal]] and [[Spain]].<ref name="Grin"/>

==Ecology==
[[File:Raphanus raphanistrum habitat.jpg|thumb|Wild radish in a cereal field margin]]
It is frost hardy, and even hard freezes only temporarily interrupt bloom. In Australia, it is regarded as a habitat threatening [[invasive species]] in many areas.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Peltzer|first1=Sally|title=Wild radish|url=https://www.agric.wa.gov.au/grains-research-development/wild-radish|publisher=Western Australia Department of Agriculture and Food|access-date=10 November 2015}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://florabase.dpaw.wa.gov.au/browse/profile/3061|title=Raphanus raphanistrum (FloraBase—the Western Australian Flora)|last=Western Australian Herbarium|first=Biodiversity and Conservation Science|website=florabase.dpaw.wa.gov.au|language=en|access-date=2020-03-20}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3040983|title=Raphanus raphanistrum L.|website=www.gbif.org|language=en|access-date=2020-03-20}}</ref> In Canada, it is a [[naturalised]] species and sometimes hybridizes with cultivated radish, ''R. sativus''. It has also proved to be resistant to several [[herbicide]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Warwick|first1=Suzanne I.|last2=Francis|first2=Ardath|title=The biology of Canadian weeds. 132. ''Raphanus raphanistrum''. L.|journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science|volume=85|issue=3|pages=709–733|date=3 February 2005|publisher=Eastern Cereal and Oilseed Research Centre|doi=10.4141/P04-120|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In southeastern USA, the pale yellow form is common, sometimes entirely taking over fields in wintertime. It is a significant source of pollen and nectar for a variety of [[pollinators]], especially [[Western honey bee|honey bees]] during the very early spring starting buildup. Female ''[[Andrena agilissima]]'', or ''mining bees'', frequent this plant to obtain pollen and nectar.<ref>{{Cite journal |title = Body size, loading capacity and rate of reproduction in the communal bee ''Andrena agilissima'' (Hymenoptera; Andrenidae)|journal = Apidologie|pages = 439–447|volume = 36|issue = 3 |date=July–September 2005 |doi = 10.1051/apido:2005028|first1 = Manuela|last1 = Giovanetti|first2 = Eloisa|last2 = Lasso|doi-access = free}}</ref> Other pollinators include [[Pieris rapae|cabbage butterflies]] and a few [[syrphid fly]] species.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Koelling|first1=Vanessa A.|last2=Karoly|first2=Keith|title=Self-pollen interference is absent in wild radish (''Raphanus raphanistrum'', Brassicaceae), a species with sporophytic self-incompatibility|journal=Am. J. Bot.|date=May 2007|volume=94|issue=5|pages=896–900|doi=10.3732/ajb.94.5.896|pmid=21636458|hdl=1808/10342|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

==Uses==
All tender parts of the plant are edible. The leaves and flowers have a spicy taste or aftertaste. The seedpods can be eaten, as can the outer skin of the root (after being washed).<ref>{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}}</ref> It is said{{By_whom|date=February 2025}} that [[John Walker (natural historian)|John Walker]] cultivated sea radish root as an alternative to [[horseradish]] after discovering the plant on the west coast of Scotland as early as 1753.<ref>{{cite book |title=English Botany: or, Coloured Figures of British Plants |last1=Sowerby |first1=James |last2=Smith |first2=James Edward |year=1806 |edition=First}}</ref>
